# WHACK Black box — Organization Profile

- **Document ID:** ORG-001
- **Author / Department:** Executive Committee
- **Date:** 2023-08-15
- **Project:** Four-season production archive
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Organization
WHACK Black box is a fictional, student-led performing-arts organization that produces one major play per academic season. It operates the WHACK Black Box Theater and WHACK Auditorium. The organization combines artistic programming, student leadership, technical production, audience development, and community engagement.

## Mission and operating model
WHACK develops collaborative theater through a repeatable production cycle: selection and dramaturgical research; director/Production Manager alignment; design-team formation; rehearsal and build; paper tech and technical rehearsals; public performances; strike; and archival closeout.

The Production Manager is the operational integrator, not the artistic supervisor of every designer. The Director owns the artistic interpretation. Stage Managers maintain the rehearsal record and call the performance. Designers own their disciplines while communicating dependencies and deadlines to the Production Manager.

## Permanent position structure per season
- 2 Production Managers
- 2 Stage Managers
- 1 Director
- 7 Actors
- 2 Costume Designers
- 5 Set & Prop Designers
- 2 Light Designers
- 2 Sound Designers
- 4 Publicity staff
- 2 Dramaturgs

Each season uses a new cohort. A role title remains stable even when its holder changes. The two Production Managers divide operational and finance/logistics responsibilities; the two Stage Managers divide rehearsal-room and calling/documentation responsibilities. Designer teams divide scope by agreed work packages rather than duplicating ownership.

## Venues
- **WHACK Black Box Theater:** flexible seating, intimate sightlines, limited backstage storage, and short audience-to-stage distance.
- **WHACK Auditorium:** wider playing area, larger audience capacity, longer cable runs, and more complex audience/house coordination.

## Donor and vendor continuity
The recurring donors are Marlowe Arts Fund, Northbridge Community Foundation, and Evelyn Hart Memorial Fund. Recurring vendors are Beacon Scenic Supply, Harborlight Costume & Textiles, Signal Path Audio, Lumen Stage Services, Cambridge Print Cooperative, and Westside Prop House. No vendor commitment is valid until the approval workflow is complete.

## Institutional lessons carried forward
1. Freeze high-risk scenic dimensions before ordering materials.
2. Use a written prop preset and return log for fragile or borrowed objects.
3. Put all cue changes in the Stage Manager's master script; verbal-only changes are not authoritative.
4. Reserve a contingency line in each production budget rather than treating it as available design money.
5. Close each season with a documented strike inventory and a short lessons-learned review.

- **Approval status:** Approved

## Donors
- **Marlowe Arts Fund:** annual unrestricted arts education grant. Acknowledgment language and any donor restrictions must be reviewed before public use.
- **Northbridge Community Foundation:** seasonal community-engagement support. Acknowledgment language and any donor restrictions must be reviewed before public use.
- **Evelyn Hart Memorial Fund:** restricted support for student artist development. Acknowledgment language and any donor restrictions must be reviewed before public use.

## Vendors
- **Beacon Scenic Supply:** lumber, paint, hardware, and scenic materials. Obtain a written quote and retain an itemized receipt for every purchase.
- **Harborlight Costume & Textiles:** fabric, notions, rentals, and alterations. Obtain a written quote and retain an itemized receipt for every purchase.
- **Signal Path Audio:** audio equipment rental and cable repair. Obtain a written quote and retain an itemized receipt for every purchase.
- **Lumen Stage Services:** lighting fixtures, lamps, and specialty rental. Obtain a written quote and retain an itemized receipt for every purchase.
- **Cambridge Print Cooperative:** posters, programs, and large-format printing. Obtain a written quote and retain an itemized receipt for every purchase.
- **Westside Prop House:** period furniture, hand props, and specialty objects. Obtain a written quote and retain an itemized receipt for every purchase.

## Continuity notes
The same donor and vendor organizations recur throughout all four seasons. This does not imply that every vendor is used for every production. Vendor selection depends on the production's needs, quote, delivery date, and approved budget. Staff should not promise donor recognition placement or vendor payment dates without confirming the relevant approval.

title: Sponsorship, Purchase, and Reimbursement Approval Workflow
document_type: Sponsorship and Purchase Approval Workflow
author: Finance & Operations Committee
body:
# Sponsorship, Purchase, and Reimbursement Approval Workflow

- **Document ID:** ORG-004
- **Author / Department:** Finance & Operations Committee
- **Date:** 2023-08-25
- **Project:** WHACK four-season production operations
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Purpose
This workflow applies to donor support, vendor commitments, purchases, rentals, reimbursements, and sponsor recognition for all WHACK productions.

## Roles and decision rights
1. **Requesting employee / designer:** submits purpose, item or service, quantity, quote, needed-by date, production code, and proposed budget line. The requester must disclose whether the item is borrowed, rented, consumable, or reusable.
2. **Relevant department lead:** confirms artistic/technical necessity and scope. For a designer purchase, the relevant designer lead confirms specifications; the Director confirms alignment with the production concept.
3. **Production Manager (PM):** checks schedule, budget availability, alternatives, storage, delivery access, and whether the request creates a technical dependency. One PM maintains the master budget; the second PM maintains purchasing and logistics records.
4. **Finance Coordinator:** confirms donor restrictions, cash availability, receipt requirements, and vendor payment method.
5. **Executive Committee:** approves exceptions, unbudgeted commitments, donor-facing promises, and purchases that exceed the delegated threshold.
6. **Stage Manager (SM):** receives approved delivery/preset information when it affects rehearsal, backstage traffic, props, costumes, or cues.

## Approval thresholds
- Up to $75 within an approved line: PM approval plus receipt.
- $75.01–$250 within an approved line: both PMs approve; Finance Coordinator records the commitment.
- Above $250, any unbudgeted purchase, or any recurring service commitment: Executive Committee approval before order.
- Any donor-restricted expenditure: Finance Coordinator verifies eligibility before a commitment, regardless of amount.

## Donor acknowledgment
Marlowe Arts Fund receives a standard season acknowledgment in the printed program and season report. Northbridge Community Foundation receives a community-engagement acknowledgment. Evelyn Hart Memorial Fund is acknowledged only in connection with student artist-development activity. Do not imply a donor endorses a particular artistic interpretation.

## Required record fields
Every request must include: request ID; season and production; requester; vendor; description; quote; budget line; requested date; approvers; decision; order date; delivery date; receipt link or filename; and closeout status.

## Exception handling
If a delivery is late or an item is unavailable, the PM documents the risk, proposes a substitute, and obtains designer/director confirmation before changing the design. A verbal okay does not replace a written approval. If an emergency purchase is required to protect safety or keep a performance running, the PM records the reason and obtains retrospective Finance/Executive review within two business days.

## Institutional rationale
The workflow is designed to protect both artistic intent and institutional stewardship. Early quotes prevent rushed purchases; written approvals preserve decision history; and the receipt trail makes it possible for the next season's team to understand actual costs rather than relying on memory.

title: Four-Season Institutional Knowledge and Continuity Memo
document_type: Four Season Institutional Lessons
author: Operations & Records
body:
# Four-Season Institutional Knowledge and Continuity Memo

- **Document ID:** ORG-005
- **Author / Department:** Operations & Records
- **Date:** 2027-03-15
- **Project:** WHACK four-season production archive
- **Approval status:** Approved for archive

## Purpose
This memo preserves operational lessons across the four productions without implying that artistic solutions should be copied from one play to another.

## Cross-season patterns
- **Hamlet (2023–2024):** intimate sightlines and the Ghost effect reinforced the need to test visibility and performer traffic in the actual black box. The team formalized the principle that a supernatural effect should be repeatable and safe before it is made more elaborate.
- **A Midsummer Night's Dream (2024–2025):** the auditorium's wider stage and longer cable paths made venue-specific planning essential. Ground-supported forest units replaced overhead scenic ideas, demonstrating that a constraint can strengthen a coherent design.
- **The Glass Menagerie (2025–2026):** fragile glass-animal props required named handoff owners, a protected storage location, and two-person inventory at strike. The team learned to treat fragile props as tracked assets, not decorative objects.
- **Macbeth (2026–2027):** blood effects, dagger props, and fight sequences required repeatable preset, cleanup, and choreography controls. Safety notes belonged in the prompt book and production records, not only in individual memory.

## Institutional practices retained
1. A written PM/Director responsibility agreement precedes design work.
2. Each designer submits a timeline, progress updates, and strike needs.
3. The PM maintains the budget and schedule; designers own their craft; the SM owns the prompt book and calling script.
4. The caller's master script is the authoritative cue record.
5. All purchases follow ORG-004, including donor restriction checks.
6. Every borrowed item has an owner, condition record, and return deadline.
7. The closeout packet includes final files, receipts, inventory, and lessons learned.

## What should not be copied blindly
A scenic unit, cue, costume treatment, or publicity plan that worked for one production is not automatically appropriate for another. Future teams should reuse the documentation method and verify the current script, venue, budget, and safety conditions.

# Data Dictionary and Relationship Guide

- **Document ID:** ORG-006
- **Author / Department:** Knowledge Systems Working Group
- **Date:** 2027-03-20
- **Project:** WHACK organizational memory prototype
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Metadata fields
- `Document ID`: globally unique record identifier.
- `Author / Department`: person and role responsible for the record.
- `Date`: authored or last materially updated date.
- `Project`: production title and season.
- `Season`: academic season identifier.
- `Venue`: physical production venue.
- `Approval status`: Approved, Approved minutes, Internal working record, Filed, or another explicit state.
- `Employee ID`: stable employee identifier within the corpus.
- `Related season records`: explicit links to connected records.

## Entity types
Organization; Season; Production; Venue; Employee; Position; Department; Donor; Vendor; Purchase Request; Approval; Meeting; Task; Risk; Cue; Prop; Costume; Scenic Unit; Rehearsal; Performance; Closeout.

## Relationship examples
- Employee `ASSIGNED_TO` Position during Season.
- Season `PRESENTS` Production.
- Production `STAGED_AT` Venue.
- Employee `AUTHORED` Document.
- Meeting `DECIDED` Decision.
- Decision `AFFECTS` Task or Budget Line.
- Purchase Request `REQUESTED_FROM` Vendor.
- Approval `AUTHORIZED_BY` Approver.
- Donor `SUPPORTS` Eligible Activity.
- Closeout `PRESERVES` Lesson for later seasons.

## Ingestion recommendations
Chunk each Markdown file by second-level heading where possible. Retain the metadata header with each chunk. Treat employee ID, season, production, and document ID as filterable metadata. Resolve repeated names through employee IDs, not names alone. Do not infer approval from the presence of a purchase in a progress report.

title: Hamlet — Event / Production Brief
document_type: Event Brief
author: June Whitaker (Director) with Mira Chen and Elias Porter (Production Managers)
body:
# Hamlet — Event / Production Brief

- **Document ID:** S1-01
- **Author / Department:** June Whitaker (Director) with Mira Chen and Elias Porter (Production Managers)
- **Date:** 2023-08-28
- **Project:** Hamlet — WHACK 2023-2024 Season
- **Season:** 2023-2024
- **Venue:** WHACK Black Box Theater
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Purpose
Produce one fully staged WHACK production for the 2023-2024 season, with public performances October 19–22, 2023 at WHACK Black Box Theater.

## Artistic and production concept
A court where surveillance has become ordinary: Elsinore is a beautiful but watchful institution, with translucent scrims, narrow sightlines, and a persistent sense that every private conversation may be overheard.

- **Design palette:** cold slate, tarnished gold, and bruised blue
- **Scenic approach:** modular court platform, two rolling benches, translucent upstage scrim, and a removable platform for the play-within-the-play
- **Sound approach:** low room tone, distant bells, wind through stone corridors, and a restrained transition motif
- **Lighting approach:** hard side light, narrow specials, and a cold backlight for the Ghost
- **Costume approach:** contemporary formal silhouettes with restrained early-modern references; court rank expressed through fabric and condition

## Production-specific risk
The Ghost effect must read clearly without creating an unsafe or unreliable performer entrance; sword work must be repeatable and choreographed.


## Scope and success criteria
- Deliver the script's full dramatic arc while maintaining safe, repeatable staging.
- Complete design handoff, build, fittings, cue programming, and paper tech by the dates in the production calendar.
- Maintain a balanced budget with documented approvals and receipts.
- Provide accessible audience circulation and a clear house-management plan.
- Complete strike, borrowed-item returns, and archival handoff within 48 hours of the final performance.

## Key personnel
- Director: June Whitaker
- Production Managers: Mira Chen (budget and schedule) and Elias Porter (purchasing, facilities, and vendor coordination)
- Stage Managers: Nadia Brooks (rehearsal reports and prompt book) and Theo Alvarez (calling script, props/costume tracking, and performance coverage)

## Milestones
- Concept and role-alignment meeting: 2023-08-28
- Design package and preliminary quotes: 6 weeks before opening
- Design freeze / final measurements: 4 weeks before opening
- Build and acquisition substantially complete: 2 weeks before opening
- Paper tech: 10 days before opening
- Cue-to-cue and technical rehearsals: final 7 days
- Invited dress: 2 days before opening
- Opening: 2023-10-19
- Strike and inventory: within 48 hours after closing

## Budget framework
Planning cap: $4,800. This is a planning ceiling, not permission to spend. A $480 contingency reserve is held by Finance and may be released only through the approval workflow. Final spending and restricted donor allocations are recorded in the season budget report.

## Audience and publicity
Publicity will coordinate posters, program, production photographs, digital announcements, and house management. Publicity copy must be checked against the Director's approved synopsis and dramaturgical fact sheet.

## Approval
Approved by Director June Whitaker and Production Managers Mira Chen / Elias Porter. Any scope change affecting safety, schedule, or budget requires a dated change note.

# Previous Sponsorship Proposal and Season Lessons — Hamlet

- **Project:** Hamlet — WHACK 2023-2024 Season
- **Season:** 2023-2024
- **Venue:** WHACK Black Box Theater

## Historical context
No prior WHACK production proposal is included in this four-season archive. The team uses the approved season planning cap and records its first complete cost baseline.

## Sponsorship case
WHACK requests continued support for a single-season production that combines student artistic development, technical training, and public access to live theater. Donor support is translated into specific, trackable production needs rather than a general promise of visibility.

## Recurring supporters
- Marlowe Arts Fund: unrestricted arts education support; proposed acknowledgment in the printed program and season report.
- Northbridge Community Foundation: community-engagement support; proposed acknowledgment alongside outreach activity.
- Evelyn Hart Memorial Fund: student artist-development support; recognition limited to the eligible training and development activity.

## Budget precedent
Initial baseline only; actuals will be established at closeout.

## Proposed use of funds
- Scenic materials and hardware: $1,150
- Costume materials, rentals, and alterations: $650
- Lighting and sound rentals/repairs: $700
- Props and specialty items: $450
- Printing and publicity: $350
- Rehearsal/production consumables: $300
- Contingency held by Finance: $480
- Remaining planned labor/training and access costs: $720

## Lessons and recommendations
1. Seek quotes from the recurring vendors early, but compare availability and total delivery cost.
2. Do not use restricted student-development funds to cover general scenic purchases.
3. Confirm photo dates before promising a print deadline.
4. Preserve at least one reusable scenic or prop component where it does not compromise the production's concept.
5. Record why a rejected alternative was rejected; the next team should not have to rediscover the same constraint.

## Decision requested
Continue the recurring donor acknowledgment framework and approve a planning ceiling of $4,800, subject to the separate purchase approval workflow. This proposal is not itself a purchase authorization.

1. **Concept translation:** June Whitaker presented the concept: A court where surveillance has become ordinary: Elsinore is a beautiful but watchful institution, with translucent scrims, narrow sightlines, and a persistent sense that every private conversation may be overheard.

- Design leads: submit initial drawings, cue concepts, or costume renderings by the design review.

## Performance notes
Record missed/late cues, prop or costume repairs, audience-flow issues, and any change made to the running sequence. Distinguish one-time irregularities from changes that should become permanent.

## Preset and strike
All props and costumes are checked against the preset list before each performance. At strike, items are sorted into return, storage, repair, and disposal categories. Fragile or borrowed items are counted by two people.

## Lessons for future Stage Managers
- Use a single source of truth for cues and blocking.
- Photograph complex presets before the first performance.
- Keep a written shift checklist for every transition.

# Director's Concept and Rehearsal Priorities — June Whitaker

- **Document ID:** S1-EMP-WH-01-005-01
- **Author / Department:** June Whitaker (Director)

- **Project:** Hamlet — WHACK 2023-2024 Season

- **Employee ID:** WH-01-005
- **Position:** Director
- **Department:** Director
- **Related season records:** S1-01 Event Brief; S1-03 Meeting Notes; S1-04 Status Report; S1-05 Change Log.

## Directorial premise
A court where surveillance has become ordinary: Elsinore is a beautiful but watchful institution, with translucent scrims, narrow sightlines, and a persistent sense that every private conversation may be overheard.

## Dramatic priorities
The production must preserve the play's central conflicts and character relationships while making the staging legible in this venue. The design should support rather than illustrate every line.

## Collaboration agreements
I will communicate interpretive decisions to the PMs and department heads early enough for them to test feasibility. If a concept changes after design freeze, I will submit a change request with the PM and identify effects on budget, schedule, safety, and other departments.

## Production-specific questions
- What must the audience understand at the moment of the central turning point?
- Which transitions should feel seamless, and which should be visibly theatrical?
- What information should costume, light, sound, and scenic design convey without dialogue?
- What must remain safe and repeatable across every performance?

## Rehearsal priorities
Actors should pursue playable objectives and clear shifts rather than generalized emotion. Blocking should be repeatable and must respect the approved scenic traffic plan.

## Design decisions
- Scenic: modular court platform, two rolling benches, translucent upstage scrim, and a removable platform for the play-within-the-play
- Costumes: contemporary formal silhouettes with restrained early-modern references; court rank expressed through fabric and condition
- Lighting: hard side light, narrow specials, and a cold backlight for the Ghost
- Sound: low room tone, distant bells, wind through stone corridors, and a restrained transition motif

## Decision log
I will record any change to concept, scene transition, or staging that affects another department. The PMs will assess operational impact; the SMs will update the prompt book and calling script.

## Collaboration reflection
A useful production meeting makes uncertainty visible early. I will identify what is a firm artistic requirement, what is an experiment, and what may be simplified if time or budget becomes constrained.

## Employee and assignment

- **Position:** Costume Designer
- **Department:** Costume Designer
- **Related season records:** S1-01 Event Brief; S1-03 Meeting Notes; S1-04 Status Report; S1-05 Change Log.

## Scope of responsibility
As Costume Designer, I own the following work package: character costume plot, fittings, alterations, laundry/repair plan, quick-change tracking, and borrowed-item return log.

## Production-specific brief
- Costume language: contemporary formal silhouettes with restrained early-modern references; court rank expressed through fabric and condition
- Track silhouette, fabric, color, wear, and status changes by character.
- For each costume, record source (owned, borrowed, rented, purchased, built), fitting status, alteration, and return deadline.
- Confirm movement, visibility, and quick-change feasibility with actors and SMs.
- Coordinate purchases with Harborlight Costume & Textiles and the PM approval workflow.

## Coordination and deadlines
I will meet the Director and PMs at concept review, submit a preliminary package at design review, identify dependencies before design freeze, attend relevant paper tech/technical rehearsals, and provide a strike/closeout list.

## Decision rules
No purchase, rental, or vendor commitment is made before approval. Any change that affects another department is sent to the PM and SM in writing. Safety and repeatability take priority over an untested late addition.

title: A Midsummer Night's Dream — Event / Production Brief
document_type: Event Brief
author: Lucas Bennett (Director) with Ari Kaplan and Sienna Brooks (Production Managers)
project: A Midsummer Night's Dream — WHACK 2024-2025 Season
body:
# A Midsummer Night's Dream — Event / Production Brief

- **Document ID:** S2-01
- **Author / Department:** Lucas Bennett (Director) with Ari Kaplan and Sienna Brooks (Production Managers)
- **Date:** 2024-09-09
- **Project:** A Midsummer Night's Dream — WHACK 2024-2025 Season
- **Season:** 2024-2025
- **Venue:** WHACK Auditorium
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Purpose
Produce one fully staged WHACK production for the 2024-2025 season, with public performances March 6–9, 2025 at WHACK Auditorium.

## Artistic and production concept
Two worlds collide: the court is orderly and geometric, while the forest is handmade, tactile, and slightly unruly. The audience should feel the forest gradually taking over the room.

- **Design palette:** warm ivory and forest green shifting to saturated violet, amber, and moonlit blue
- **Scenic approach:** lightweight forest arches, fabric canopy, movable tree units, and a clear central playing area for safe physical comedy
- **Sound approach:** layered night insects, live-feeling percussion textures, and distinct transition cues for the lovers' confusion
- **Lighting approach:** broad court washes giving way to dappled forest textures, gobos, and a soft moon special
- **Costume approach:** court garments in clean lines; fairies in layered natural textures; mechanicals in visibly improvised work clothes

## Production-specific risk
The auditorium has a wider stage and longer cable runs; flying or overhead scenic elements are prohibited, so all forest transformations must be ground-supported.


## Scope and success criteria
- Deliver the script's full dramatic arc while maintaining safe, repeatable staging.
- Complete design handoff, build, fittings, cue programming, and paper tech by the dates in the production calendar.
- Maintain a balanced budget with documented approvals and receipts.
- Provide accessible audience circulation and a clear house-management plan.
- Complete strike, borrowed-item returns, and archival handoff within 48 hours of the final performance.

## Key personnel
- Director: Lucas Bennett
- Production Managers: Ari Kaplan (budget and schedule) and Sienna Brooks (purchasing, facilities, and vendor coordination)
- Stage Managers: Devon Clarke (rehearsal reports and prompt book) and Hana Mori (calling script, props/costume tracking, and performance coverage)

## Milestones
- Concept and role-alignment meeting: 2024-09-09
- Design package and preliminary quotes: 6 weeks before opening
- Design freeze / final measurements: 4 weeks before opening
- Build and acquisition substantially complete: 2 weeks before opening
- Paper tech: 10 days before opening
- Cue-to-cue and technical rehearsals: final 7 days
- Invited dress: 2 days before opening
- Opening: 2025-03-06
- Strike and inventory: within 48 hours after closing

## Budget framework
Planning cap: $4,800. This is a planning ceiling, not permission to spend. A $480 contingency reserve is held by Finance and may be released only through the approval workflow. Final spending and restricted donor allocations are recorded in the season budget report.

## Audience and publicity
Publicity will coordinate posters, program, production photographs, digital announcements, and house management. Publicity copy must be checked against the Director's approved synopsis and dramaturgical fact sheet.

## Approval
Approved by Director Lucas Bennett and Production Managers Ari Kaplan / Sienna Brooks. Any scope change affecting safety, schedule, or budget requires a dated change note.

title: Previous Sponsorship Proposal and Season Lessons — A Midsummer Night's Dream
document_type: Previous Season Proposal and Lessons
author: Ari Kaplan / Finance & Operations
project: A Midsummer Night's Dream — WHACK 2024-2025 Season
body:
# Previous Sponsorship Proposal and Season Lessons — A Midsummer Night's Dream

- **Document ID:** S2-02
- **Author / Department:** Ari Kaplan / Finance & Operations
- **Date:** 2024-09-09
- **Project:** A Midsummer Night's Dream — WHACK 2024-2025 Season
- **Season:** 2024-2025
- **Venue:** WHACK Auditorium
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Historical context
The previous season's Hamlet closed with a documented lesson: The Ghost effect must read clearly without creating an unsafe or unreliable performer entrance; sword work must be repeatable and choreographed. The current team carries forward the practice of freezing high-risk design details before ordering.

## Sponsorship case
WHACK requests continued support for a single-season production that combines student artistic development, technical training, and public access to live theater. Donor support is translated into specific, trackable production needs rather than a general promise of visibility.

## Recurring supporters
- Marlowe Arts Fund: unrestricted arts education support; proposed acknowledgment in the printed program and season report.
- Northbridge Community Foundation: community-engagement support; proposed acknowledgment alongside outreach activity.
- Evelyn Hart Memorial Fund: student artist-development support; recognition limited to the eligible training and development activity.

## Budget precedent
Prior production: Hamlet (2023-2024); planning cap $4,800; contingency reserve $480; actual category totals are retained in the prior season's closeout report.

## Proposed use of funds
- Scenic materials and hardware: $1,150
- Costume materials, rentals, and alterations: $650
- Lighting and sound rentals/repairs: $700
- Props and specialty items: $450
- Printing and publicity: $350
- Rehearsal/production consumables: $300
- Contingency held by Finance: $480
- Remaining planned labor/training and access costs: $720

## Lessons and recommendations
1. Seek quotes from the recurring vendors early, but compare availability and total delivery cost.
2. Do not use restricted student-development funds to cover general scenic purchases.
3. Confirm photo dates before promising a print deadline.
4. Preserve at least one reusable scenic or prop component where it does not compromise the production's concept.
5. Record why a rejected alternative was rejected; the next team should not have to rediscover the same constraint.

## Decision requested
Continue the recurring donor acknowledgment framework and approve a planning ceiling of $4,800, subject to the separate purchase approval workflow. This proposal is not itself a purchase authorization.

- **Approval status:** Approved minutes

## Attendees
Director Lucas Bennett; PMs Ari Kaplan and Sienna Brooks; SMs Devon Clarke and Hana Mori; department design leads; dramaturgs.

## Discussion and decisions
1. **Concept translation:** Lucas Bennett presented the concept: Two worlds collide: the court is orderly and geometric, while the forest is handmade, tactile, and slightly unruly. The audience should feel the forest gradually taking over the room.
2. **Scenic scope:** Set & Prop team will submit a measured ground plan and a list of borrowed versus purchased items. No order may be placed before PM review.
3. **Costume scope:** Costume team will schedule fittings after the first complete character/scene breakdown. Any quick-change risk must be flagged to both SMs.
4. **Lighting and sound:** Designers will deliver preliminary cue families before paper tech. The Stage Manager's calling script will be the authoritative cue record.
5. **Dramaturgy:** Dramaturgs will prepare a source-checked fact sheet and a short audience-facing synopsis. Publicity must use the approved synopsis.
6. **Schedule:** PMs will circulate a master calendar and weekly risk list. Each department lead will report red/amber/green status at the weekly production meeting.

## Action items
- Ari Kaplan: open the master budget and reserve ledger; due one week after kickoff.
- Sienna Brooks: obtain written quotes from relevant recurring vendors; due two weeks after kickoff.
- Devon Clarke: establish rehearsal-report distribution and attendance tracking.
- Hana Mori: create prompt-book structure and preset/shift tracking sheets.
- Director Lucas Bennett: approve the one-paragraph concept statement and final synopsis.
- Design leads: submit initial drawings, cue concepts, or costume renderings by the design review.

## Rationale captured
The team agreed that early written design decisions reduce last-minute substitutions. The previous proposal's recommendation to freeze dimensions before purchasing is retained because late changes create both cost and safety risks.

## Open questions
- Final count of specialty rentals remains pending vendor quotes.
- Publicity photo call depends on the first complete costume and scenic mock-up.
- Any safety-sensitive staging will be reviewed before it is incorporated into the blocking.

## Delegated approvals
This season follows ORG-004. Requests up to $75 within an approved line require PM approval and receipt; $75.01–$250 require both PMs; larger, unbudgeted, recurring, or restricted-fund commitments require Executive Committee/Finance review.

## Change request protocol
A change request must identify the originating document, explain the proposed revision, state cost and schedule impact, identify safety implications, and name the person responsible for updating dependent records. If approved, the PM updates the budget and schedule, and the SM updates rehearsal/prompt-book records where applicable.

## Decision history principle
The team records not only what was decided but why. A later season may face a different artistic problem, but it should be able to distinguish a deliberate precedent from an accidental habit.

# Director's Concept and Rehearsal Priorities — Lucas Bennett

- **Document ID:** S2-EMP-WH-02-005-01

- **Position:** Director

## Directorial premise
Two worlds collide: the court is orderly and geometric, while the forest is handmade, tactile, and slightly unruly. The audience should feel the forest gradually taking over the room.

## Dramatic priorities
The production must preserve the play's central conflicts and character relationships while making the staging legible in this venue. The design should support rather than illustrate every line.

## Collaboration agreements
I will communicate interpretive decisions to the PMs and department heads early enough for them to test feasibility. If a concept changes after design freeze, I will submit a change request with the PM and identify effects on budget, schedule, safety, and other departments.

## Production-specific questions
- What must the audience understand at the moment of the central turning point?
- Which transitions should feel seamless, and which should be visibly theatrical?
- What information should costume, light, sound, and scenic design convey without dialogue?
- What must remain safe and repeatable across every performance?

## Rehearsal priorities

## Design decisions
- Scenic: lightweight forest arches, fabric canopy, movable tree units, and a clear central playing area for safe physical comedy
- Costumes: court garments in clean lines; fairies in layered natural textures; mechanicals in visibly improvised work clothes
- Lighting: broad court washes giving way to dappled forest textures, gobos, and a soft moon special
- Sound: layered night insects, live-feeling percussion textures, and distinct transition cues for the lovers' confusion

## Decision log
I will record any change to concept, scene transition, or staging that affects another department. The PMs will assess operational impact; the SMs will update the prompt book and calling script.

## Collaboration reflection
A useful production meeting makes uncertainty visible early. I will identify what is a firm artistic requirement, what is an experiment, and what may be simplified if time or budget becomes constrained.

## Artistic assessment
The production's strongest moments were those in which actor action and design language reinforced the same dramatic idea. The most useful production lesson concerns: The auditorium has a wider stage and longer cable runs; flying or overhead scenic elements are prohibited, so all forest transformations must be ground-supported.

## What should be preserved
Keep the final approved concept statement, the final blocking version, and the cue/transition notes together. A future team may reuse a technical method without repeating this production's artistic interpretation.

- What does the character want in each scene?

The design concept is: Two worlds collide: the court is orderly and geometric, while the forest is handmade, tactile, and slightly unruly. The audience should feel the forest gradually taking over the room.
I will identify costume, prop, sound, and scenic interactions that affect my movement. I will not independently alter a prop, costume, or fight sequence; I will bring the question to the SM and relevant designer.

Arrive with script, pencil, water, and completed assigned reading. Record blocking in the script and report conflicts, discomfort, or safety concerns promptly.

# The Glass Menagerie — Event / Production Brief

- **Document ID:** S3-01
- **Author / Department:** Mina Alvarez (Director) with Riley Morgan and Amir Patel (Production Managers)
- **Date:** 2025-08-25
- **Project:** The Glass Menagerie — WHACK 2025-2026 Season
- **Season:** 2025-2026
- **Venue:** WHACK Black Box Theater
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Purpose
Produce one fully staged WHACK production for the 2025-2026 season, with public performances November 13–16, 2025 at WHACK Black Box Theater.

## Artistic and production concept
A memory play in which the apartment is both specific and unstable. The set should suggest a cramped St. Louis tenement without pretending that memory is realistic or complete.

- **Design palette:** smoky amber, faded rose, and translucent gray
- **Scenic approach:** compact fire-escape unit, narrow dining table, practical lamp, and a dedicated glass-animal display surface; all paths remain accessible
- **Sound approach:** subtle streetcar and fire-escape ambience, restrained music transitions, and silence protected around key monologues
- **Lighting approach:** isolated memory pools, soft edge light, and selective dimming to make scenes appear and disappear
- **Costume approach:** 1930s-inspired everyday clothing with deliberate wear, repairs, and small details that distinguish memory from present action

## Production-specific risk
The glass menagerie props are fragile and must have a controlled handoff and storage protocol; the fire-escape unit requires load and stability checks.


## Scope and success criteria
- Deliver the script's full dramatic arc while maintaining safe, repeatable staging.
- Complete design handoff, build, fittings, cue programming, and paper tech by the dates in the production calendar.
- Maintain a balanced budget with documented approvals and receipts.
- Provide accessible audience circulation and a clear house-management plan.
- Complete strike, borrowed-item returns, and archival handoff within 48 hours of the final performance.

## Key personnel
- Director: Mina Alvarez
- Production Managers: Riley Morgan (budget and schedule) and Amir Patel (purchasing, facilities, and vendor coordination)
- Stage Managers: Clara Hughes (rehearsal reports and prompt book) and Jasper Lee (calling script, props/costume tracking, and performance coverage)

## Milestones
- Concept and role-alignment meeting: 2025-08-25
- Design package and preliminary quotes: 6 weeks before opening
- Design freeze / final measurements: 4 weeks before opening
- Build and acquisition substantially complete: 2 weeks before opening
- Paper tech: 10 days before opening
- Cue-to-cue and technical rehearsals: final 7 days
- Invited dress: 2 days before opening
- Opening: 2025-11-13
- Strike and inventory: within 48 hours after closing

## Budget framework
Planning cap: $4,800. This is a planning ceiling, not permission to spend. A $480 contingency reserve is held by Finance and may be released only through the approval workflow. Final spending and restricted donor allocations are recorded in the season budget report.

## Audience and publicity
Publicity will coordinate posters, program, production photographs, digital announcements, and house management. Publicity copy must be checked against the Director's approved synopsis and dramaturgical fact sheet.

## Approval
Approved by Director Mina Alvarez and Production Managers Riley Morgan / Amir Patel. Any scope change affecting safety, schedule, or budget requires a dated change note.

title: Previous Sponsorship Proposal and Season Lessons — The Glass Menagerie
document_type: Previous Season Proposal and Lessons
author: Riley Morgan / Finance & Operations
body:
# Previous Sponsorship Proposal and Season Lessons — The Glass Menagerie

- **Document ID:** S3-02
- **Author / Department:** Riley Morgan / Finance & Operations
- **Date:** 2025-08-25
- **Project:** The Glass Menagerie — WHACK 2025-2026 Season
- **Season:** 2025-2026
- **Venue:** WHACK Black Box Theater
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Historical context
The previous season's A Midsummer Night's Dream closed with a documented lesson: The auditorium has a wider stage and longer cable runs; flying or overhead scenic elements are prohibited, so all forest transformations must be ground-supported. The current team carries forward the practice of freezing high-risk design details before ordering.

## Sponsorship case
WHACK requests continued support for a single-season production that combines student artistic development, technical training, and public access to live theater. Donor support is translated into specific, trackable production needs rather than a general promise of visibility.

## Recurring supporters
- Marlowe Arts Fund: unrestricted arts education support; proposed acknowledgment in the printed program and season report.
- Northbridge Community Foundation: community-engagement support; proposed acknowledgment alongside outreach activity.
- Evelyn Hart Memorial Fund: student artist-development support; recognition limited to the eligible training and development activity.

## Budget precedent
Prior production: A Midsummer Night's Dream (2024-2025); planning cap $4,800; contingency reserve $480; actual category totals are retained in the prior season's closeout report.

## Proposed use of funds
- Scenic materials and hardware: $1,150
- Costume materials, rentals, and alterations: $650
- Lighting and sound rentals/repairs: $700
- Props and specialty items: $450
- Printing and publicity: $350
- Rehearsal/production consumables: $300
- Contingency held by Finance: $480
- Remaining planned labor/training and access costs: $720

## Lessons and recommendations
1. Seek quotes from the recurring vendors early, but compare availability and total delivery cost.
2. Do not use restricted student-development funds to cover general scenic purchases.
3. Confirm photo dates before promising a print deadline.
4. Preserve at least one reusable scenic or prop component where it does not compromise the production's concept.
5. Record why a rejected alternative was rejected; the next team should not have to rediscover the same constraint.

## Decision requested
Continue the recurring donor acknowledgment framework and approve a planning ceiling of $4,800, subject to the separate purchase approval workflow. This proposal is not itself a purchase authorization.

# Kickoff and Design Meeting Notes — The Glass Menagerie

- **Document ID:** S3-03
- **Author / Department:** Clara Hughes (Stage Manager)
- **Date:** 2025-08-25
- **Project:** The Glass Menagerie — WHACK 2025-2026 Season
- **Season:** 2025-2026
- **Venue:** WHACK Black Box Theater
- **Approval status:** Approved minutes

## Attendees
Director Mina Alvarez; PMs Riley Morgan and Amir Patel; SMs Clara Hughes and Jasper Lee; department design leads; dramaturgs.

## Discussion and decisions
1. **Concept translation:** Mina Alvarez presented the concept: A memory play in which the apartment is both specific and unstable. The set should suggest a cramped St. Louis tenement without pretending that memory is realistic or complete.
2. **Scenic scope:** Set & Prop team will submit a measured ground plan and a list of borrowed versus purchased items. No order may be placed before PM review.
3. **Costume scope:** Costume team will schedule fittings after the first complete character/scene breakdown. Any quick-change risk must be flagged to both SMs.
4. **Lighting and sound:** Designers will deliver preliminary cue families before paper tech. The Stage Manager's calling script will be the authoritative cue record.
5. **Dramaturgy:** Dramaturgs will prepare a source-checked fact sheet and a short audience-facing synopsis. Publicity must use the approved synopsis.
6. **Schedule:** PMs will circulate a master calendar and weekly risk list. Each department lead will report red/amber/green status at the weekly production meeting.

## Action items
- Riley Morgan: open the master budget and reserve ledger; due one week after kickoff.
- Amir Patel: obtain written quotes from relevant recurring vendors; due two weeks after kickoff.
- Clara Hughes: establish rehearsal-report distribution and attendance tracking.
- Jasper Lee: create prompt-book structure and preset/shift tracking sheets.
- Director Mina Alvarez: approve the one-paragraph concept statement and final synopsis.
- Design leads: submit initial drawings, cue concepts, or costume renderings by the design review.

## Rationale captured
The team agreed that early written design decisions reduce last-minute substitutions. The previous proposal's recommendation to freeze dimensions before purchasing is retained because late changes create both cost and safety risks.

## Open questions
- Final count of specialty rentals remains pending vendor quotes.
- Publicity photo call depends on the first complete costume and scenic mock-up.
- Any safety-sensitive staging will be reviewed before it is incorporated into the blocking.

## Executive summary
The production is in pre-production. Artistic concept and department assignments are confirmed. The principal schedule risk is timely completion of design packages and vendor quotes. No purchase is considered approved solely because it appears in this report.

## Status by workstream
| Workstream | Status | Evidence / next action |
|---|---|---|
| Artistic concept | Green | Director's concept statement recorded in S3-01 |
| Scenic and props | Amber | Ground plan and measured elevations due; confirm access and storage |
| Costumes | Amber | Character breakdown underway; fittings to follow |
| Lighting | Amber | Preliminary cue families due before paper tech |
| Sound | Amber | Cue list and playback requirements due before paper tech |
| Stage management | Green | Prompt-book and rehearsal-report templates opened |
| Publicity | Amber | Synopsis awaiting Director approval; print schedule not yet released |
| Dramaturgy | Green | Research brief underway; factual claims will be source-checked |
| Finance | Amber | Planning cap set; quotes and purchase requests still pending |

## Completed
- Director/PM role-alignment conversation.
- Production concept and venue confirmed.
- Recurring donor and vendor register reviewed.
- Initial schedule milestones placed on the master calendar.
- Department leads assigned.

## Outstanding work
- Final design packages and measured drawings.
- Vendor quotes and written purchase requests.
- Costume fitting schedule and actor measurement confirmation.
- Cue list, cue numbering convention, and paper-tech packet.
- Publicity synopsis approval, photography schedule, and print proof.
- Borrowed-item register and fragile-prop handling plan.

## Blockers and risks
1. **Design freeze risk:** late scenic dimensions may delay Beacon Scenic Supply order. Mitigation: PM will not release purchase until designer signs off on measurements.
2. **Venue access risk:** load-in windows are limited by other venue activity. Mitigation: PM2 will confirm access in writing.
3. **Cue integration risk:** cue changes made verbally may not reach the caller. Mitigation: SM2 maintains the master calling script and timestamps revisions.
4. **Budget risk:** contingency is not available for routine scope expansion. Mitigation: Finance must approve any release.

## Upcoming deadlines
- Design review: 6 weeks before opening.
- Final quotes and design freeze: 4 weeks before opening.
- Build/acquisition substantially complete: 2 weeks before opening.
- Paper tech: 10 days before opening.
- Cue-to-cue: 7 days before opening.
- Invited dress: 2 days before opening.

## Recommended next steps
PMs should conduct short one-to-one check-ins with any amber workstream, then circulate a dated decision log. The team should prioritize safety, audience clarity, and cue reliability over decorative additions that do not materially advance the concept.

# Season Approval and Change-Control Log — The Glass Menagerie

- **Season:** 2025-2026
- **Venue:** WHACK Black Box Theater
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Delegated approvals
This season follows ORG-004. Requests up to $75 within an approved line require PM approval and receipt; $75.01–$250 require both PMs; larger, unbudgeted, recurring, or restricted-fund commitments require Executive Committee/Finance review.

## Change log
| Change ID | Request | Decision | Rationale | Record owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S3-CH-001 | Establish planning cap of $4,800 | Approved as planning ceiling | Provides a common baseline while retaining a $480 reserve | Riley Morgan |
| S3-CH-002 | Use production-specific design palette | Approved | Supports consistent interpretation across design departments | Mina Alvarez |
| S3-CH-003 | Release vendor orders before final measurements | Not approved | Avoids waste and late rework | Amir Patel |

## Change request protocol
A change request must identify the originating document, explain the proposed revision, state cost and schedule impact, identify safety implications, and name the person responsible for updating dependent records. If approved, the PM updates the budget and schedule, and the SM updates rehearsal/prompt-book records where applicable.

## Decision history principle
The team records not only what was decided but why. A later season may face a different artistic problem, but it should be able to distinguish a deliberate precedent from an accidental habit.

## Directorial premise
A memory play in which the apartment is both specific and unstable. The set should suggest a cramped St. Louis tenement without pretending that memory is realistic or complete.

## Dramatic priorities
The production must preserve the play's central conflicts and character relationships while making the staging legible in this venue. The design should support rather than illustrate every line.

## Collaboration agreements
I will communicate interpretive decisions to the PMs and department heads early enough for them to test feasibility. If a concept changes after design freeze, I will submit a change request with the PM and identify effects on budget, schedule, safety, and other departments.

## Production-specific questions
- What must the audience understand at the moment of the central turning point?
- Which transitions should feel seamless, and which should be visibly theatrical?
- What information should costume, light, sound, and scenic design convey without dialogue?
- What must remain safe and repeatable across every performance?

## Rehearsal priorities
Actors should pursue playable objectives and clear shifts rather than generalized emotion. Blocking should be repeatable and must respect the approved scenic traffic plan.

## Design decisions
- Scenic: compact fire-escape unit, narrow dining table, practical lamp, and a dedicated glass-animal display surface; all paths remain accessible
- Costumes: 1930s-inspired everyday clothing with deliberate wear, repairs, and small details that distinguish memory from present action
- Lighting: isolated memory pools, soft edge light, and selective dimming to make scenes appear and disappear
- Sound: subtle streetcar and fire-escape ambience, restrained music transitions, and silence protected around key monologues

## Decision log
I will record any change to concept, scene transition, or staging that affects another department. The PMs will assess operational impact; the SMs will update the prompt book and calling script.

## Collaboration reflection
A useful production meeting makes uncertainty visible early. I will identify what is a firm artistic requirement, what is an experiment, and what may be simplified if time or budget becomes constrained.

title: Macbeth — Event / Production Brief
document_type: Event Brief
author: Cameron Blake (Director) with Quinn Parker and Layla Chen (Production Managers)
body:
# Macbeth — Event / Production Brief

- **Document ID:** S4-01
- **Author / Department:** Cameron Blake (Director) with Quinn Parker and Layla Chen (Production Managers)
- **Date:** 2026-09-01
- **Project:** Macbeth — WHACK 2026-2027 Season
- **Season:** 2026-2027
- **Venue:** WHACK Black Box Theater
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Purpose
Produce one fully staged WHACK production for the 2026-2027 season, with public performances February 18–21, 2027 at WHACK Black Box Theater.

## Artistic and production concept
A landscape of ambition and consequence: a stripped-down military space becomes increasingly contaminated by violence and prophecy. The supernatural is created through light, sound, and actor focus rather than complicated machinery.

- **Design palette:** charcoal, rust, bone, and a narrow band of sickly green
- **Scenic approach:** distressed platform, movable banquet table, concealed prop-safe dagger storage, and a minimal throne unit
- **Sound approach:** low-frequency storm bed, distant battle textures, and distinct sonic signatures for the witches
- **Lighting approach:** stark side light, hard shadows, and carefully timed blackouts; no strobe effects
- **Costume approach:** weathered layered garments with status changes visible through armor-like additions and damage

## Production-specific risk
Blood effects and dagger props need repeatable preset and cleanup procedures; fight choreography and sound cues must be locked before invited dress.


## Scope and success criteria
- Deliver the script's full dramatic arc while maintaining safe, repeatable staging.
- Complete design handoff, build, fittings, cue programming, and paper tech by the dates in the production calendar.
- Maintain a balanced budget with documented approvals and receipts.
- Provide accessible audience circulation and a clear house-management plan.
- Complete strike, borrowed-item returns, and archival handoff within 48 hours of the final performance.

## Key personnel
- Director: Cameron Blake
- Production Managers: Quinn Parker (budget and schedule) and Layla Chen (purchasing, facilities, and vendor coordination)
- Stage Managers: Mateo Rivera (rehearsal reports and prompt book) and Sylvie Hart (calling script, props/costume tracking, and performance coverage)

## Milestones
- Concept and role-alignment meeting: 2026-09-01
- Design package and preliminary quotes: 6 weeks before opening

# Previous Sponsorship Proposal and Season Lessons — Macbeth

- **Document ID:** S4-02
- **Author / Department:** Quinn Parker / Finance & Operations
- **Date:** 2026-09-01
- **Project:** Macbeth — WHACK 2026-2027 Season
- **Season:** 2026-2027
- **Venue:** WHACK Black Box Theater
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Historical context
The previous season's The Glass Menagerie closed with a documented lesson: The glass menagerie props are fragile and must have a controlled handoff and storage protocol; the fire-escape unit requires load and stability checks. The current team carries forward the practice of freezing high-risk design details before ordering.

## Sponsorship case
WHACK requests continued support for a single-season production that combines student artistic development, technical training, and public access to live theater. Donor support is translated into specific, trackable production needs rather than a general promise of visibility.

## Recurring supporters
- Marlowe Arts Fund: unrestricted arts education support; proposed acknowledgment in the printed program and season report.
- Northbridge Community Foundation: community-engagement support; proposed acknowledgment alongside outreach activity.
- Evelyn Hart Memorial Fund: student artist-development support; recognition limited to the eligible training and development activity.

## Budget precedent
Prior production: The Glass Menagerie (2025-2026); planning cap $4,800; contingency reserve $480; actual category totals are retained in the prior season's closeout report.

## Proposed use of funds
- Scenic materials and hardware: $1,150
- Costume materials, rentals, and alterations: $650
- Lighting and sound rentals/repairs: $700
- Props and specialty items: $450
- Printing and publicity: $350
- Rehearsal/production consumables: $300
- Contingency held by Finance: $480
- Remaining planned labor/training and access costs: $720

## Lessons and recommendations
1. Seek quotes from the recurring vendors early, but compare availability and total delivery cost.
2. Do not use restricted student-development funds to cover general scenic purchases.
3. Confirm photo dates before promising a print deadline.
4. Preserve at least one reusable scenic or prop component where it does not compromise the production's concept.
5. Record why a rejected alternative was rejected; the next team should not have to rediscover the same constraint.

## Decision requested
Continue the recurring donor acknowledgment framework and approve a planning ceiling of $4,800, subject to the separate purchase approval workflow. This proposal is not itself a purchase authorization.

## Discussion and decisions
1. **Concept translation:** Cameron Blake presented the concept: A landscape of ambition and consequence: a stripped-down military space becomes increasingly contaminated by violence and prophecy. The supernatural is created through light, sound, and actor focus rather than complicated machinery.
2. **Scenic scope:** Set & Prop team will submit a measured ground plan and a list of borrowed versus purchased items. No order may be placed before PM review.

- Quinn Parker: open the master budget and reserve ledger; due one week after kickoff.

- Design leads: submit initial drawings, cue concepts, or costume renderings by the design review.

The team agreed that early written design decisions reduce last-minute substitutions. The previous proposal's recommendation to freeze dimensions before purchasing is retained because late changes create both cost and safety risks.

# Director's Concept and Rehearsal Priorities — Cameron Blake

- **Document ID:** S4-EMP-WH-04-005-01

- **Project:** Macbeth — WHACK 2026-2027 Season

## Employee and assignment
- **Employee ID:** WH-04-005
- **Position:** Director
- **Department:** Director
- **Related season records:** S4-01 Event Brief; S4-03 Meeting Notes; S4-04 Status Report; S4-05 Change Log.

## Directorial premise
A landscape of ambition and consequence: a stripped-down military space becomes increasingly contaminated by violence and prophecy. The supernatural is created through light, sound, and actor focus rather than complicated machinery.

## Dramatic priorities
The production must preserve the play's central conflicts and character relationships while making the staging legible in this venue. The design should support rather than illustrate every line.

## Collaboration agreements
I will communicate interpretive decisions to the PMs and department heads early enough for them to test feasibility. If a concept changes after design freeze, I will submit a change request with the PM and identify effects on budget, schedule, safety, and other departments.

## Production-specific questions
- What must the audience understand at the moment of the central turning point?
- Which transitions should feel seamless, and which should be visibly theatrical?
- What information should costume, light, sound, and scenic design convey without dialogue?
- What must remain safe and repeatable across every performance?

## Rehearsal priorities
Actors should pursue playable objectives and clear shifts rather than generalized emotion. Blocking should be repeatable and must respect the approved scenic traffic plan.

## Design decisions
- Scenic: distressed platform, movable banquet table, concealed prop-safe dagger storage, and a minimal throne unit
- Costumes: weathered layered garments with status changes visible through armor-like additions and damage
- Lighting: stark side light, hard shadows, and carefully timed blackouts; no strobe effects
- Sound: low-frequency storm bed, distant battle textures, and distinct sonic signatures for the witches

## Decision log
I will record any change to concept, scene transition, or staging that affects another department. The PMs will assess operational impact; the SMs will update the prompt book and calling script.

## Collaboration reflection
A useful production meeting makes uncertainty visible early. I will identify what is a firm artistic requirement, what is an experiment, and what may be simplified if time or budget becomes constrained.

## Artistic assessment
The production's strongest moments were those in which actor action and design language reinforced the same dramatic idea. The most useful production lesson concerns: Blood effects and dagger props need repeatable preset and cleanup procedures; fight choreography and sound cues must be locked before invited dress.

## What should be preserved
Keep the final approved concept statement, the final blocking version, and the cue/transition notes together. A future team may reuse a technical method without repeating this production's artistic interpretation.

## Recommendations
1. Distinguish essential storytelling elements from optional visual embellishments.
2. Bring designers into the room early enough to observe the work.
3. Confirm that the final synopsis and program language accurately describe the production.

- **Project:** Macbeth — WHACK 2026-2027 Season
- **Season:** 2026-2027
- **Venue:** WHACK Black Box Theater
- **Approval status:** Approved

## Employee and assignment
- **Employee ID:** WH-04-013
- **Position:** Costume Designer
- **Department:** Costume Designer
- **Related season records:** S4-01 Event Brief; S4-03 Meeting Notes; S4-04 Status Report; S4-05 Change Log.

## Scope of responsibility
As Costume Designer, I own the following work package: character costume plot, fittings, alterations, laundry/repair plan, quick-change tracking, and borrowed-item return log.

## Production-specific brief
- Costume language: weathered layered garments with status changes visible through armor-like additions and damage
- Track silhouette, fabric, color, wear, and status changes by character.
- For each costume, record source (owned, borrowed, rented, purchased, built), fitting status, alteration, and return deadline.
- Confirm movement, visibility, and quick-change feasibility with actors and SMs.
- Coordinate purchases with Harborlight Costume & Textiles and the PM approval workflow.

## Coordination and deadlines
I will meet the Director and PMs at concept review, submit a preliminary package at design review, identify dependencies before design freeze, attend relevant paper tech/technical rehearsals, and provide a strike/closeout list.

## Decision rules
No purchase, rental, or vendor commitment is made before approval. Any change that affects another department is sent to the PM and SM in writing. Safety and repeatability take priority over an untested late addition.

## Employee and assignment
- **Employee ID:** WH-04-016
- **Position:** Set & Prop Designer
- **Department:** Set & Prop Designer
- **Related season records:** S4-01 Event Brief; S4-03 Meeting Notes; S4-04 Status Report; S4-05 Change Log.

## Scope of responsibility
As Set & Prop Designer, I own the following work package: scenic/prop design package, measured drawings, build/acquisition list, finish samples, preset plan, and strike inventory.

## Production-specific brief
- Scenic concept: distressed platform, movable banquet table, concealed prop-safe dagger storage, and a minimal throne unit
- Submit measured ground plan, elevations, materials list, and a clear build/borrow/rent distinction.
- Confirm all units fit the venue access route and storage constraints.
- Props must have a numbered preset, handoff owner, and safe storage location.
- Source lumber/paint/hardware from Beacon Scenic Supply and specialty items from Westside Prop House only after approval.

## Coordination and deadlines
I will meet the Director and PMs at concept review, submit a preliminary package at design review, identify dependencies before design freeze, attend relevant paper tech/technical rehearsals, and provide a strike/closeout list.

## Decision rules
No purchase, rental, or vendor commitment is made before approval. Any change that affects another department is sent to the PM and SM in writing. Safety and repeatability take priority over an untested late addition.
